claims.evidence: This is supported by tBLASTx results shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: The Pdc orthologs found in W/S-clade species and C. infanticola seem to belong to a decarboxylase family that is phylogenetically related to S. cerevisiae Aro10.
claims.source: In this case, the lower E-value appears to reflect the fact that the Pdc orthologs found in W/S-clade species and C. infanticola seem to belong to a decarboxylase family that is phylogenetically related to S. cerevisiae Aro10.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on BLAST results and phylogenetic analysis.

claims.claim: In S. cerevisiae, Aro10 acts preferentially on substrates other than pyruvate and is not involved in alcoholic fermentation.
claims.source: In S. cerevisiae, Aro10 acts preferentially on substrates other than pyruvate and is not involved in alcoholic fermentation (Kneen et al., 2011; Romagnoli et al., 2012; Vuralhan et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: The phylogeny confirmed the clustering of the W/S-clade sequences with Aro10 proteins from fungi, which indicates that PDC1 was lost in the W/S clade.
claims.source: This phylogeny (Figure 3A and B) confirmed the clustering of the W/S-clade sequences with Aro10 proteins from fungi, which indicates that PDC1 was lost in the W/S clade.
claims.evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The two Pdc1-like proteins from C. versatilis were clustered with bacterial pyruvate decarboxylases.
claims.source: Additionally, as suggested by the BLASTp results, the two Pdc1-like proteins from C. versatilis were clustered with bacterial pyruvate decarboxylases (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: All glycolytic genes were found to be present in the examined species and exhibited the expected level of similarity to S. cerevisiae query proteins.
claims.source: All glycolytic genes were examined in the same set of species and were all found to be present and to exhibit the expected level of similarity to S. cerevisiae query proteins (Figure 2—source data 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2—source data 3.

claims.claim: It is very unlikely that alcoholic fermentation genes were missed in W/S-clade species because of insufficient coverage or quality of the genome assemblies used.
claims.source: This, together with the fact that other inspected publicly available genome assemblies of W/S-clade species are of very high quality (e.g. Wickerhamiella domercqiae JCM 9478, PRJDB3620 or St. bombicola JCM 9596 from RIKEN Center), makes it very unlikely that alcoholic fermentation genes were missed in W/S-clade species because of insufficient coverage or quality of the genome assemblies used.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on genome quality assessment.

claims.claim: A considerably larger number of genes of bacterial origin was found in W/S-clade species and C. infanticola when compared with the two species more distantly related to the W/S clade.
claims.source: We found a considerably larger number of genes of bacterial origin in W/S-clade species and also in C. infanticola when compared with the two species more distantly related to the W/S clade (Su. lignohabitans and B. adeninivorans, Figure 2A, Figure 2—source data 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Alien Index analysis results shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—source data 2.

claims.claim: C. versatilis displayed the highest number of putative HGT-derived genes from bacteria (211).
claims.source: Notably, C. versatilis displayed the highest number of putative HGT-derived genes from bacteria (211), followed by W. domercqiae with 80 genes for which phylogenetic clustering with bacteria could be confirmed (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Alien Index analysis results shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: A surge of HGT events occurred in the MRCA of the W/S clade.
claims.source: Given that all W/S-clade species possess a higher number of HGT-derived genes when compared to their closest relatives, it is possible that a surge of HGT events occurred in the MRCA of the W/S clade.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the distribution of HGT-derived genes across species.

claims.claim: 52 ortholog groups with representatives in two or more W/S-clade genomes were defined.
claims.source: Indeed, after implementation of alignment thresholds (protein sequences > 150 amino acids) and collapsing the replicate phylogenies and lineage-specific gene duplications, it was possible to define 52 ortholog groups with representatives in two or more W/S-clade genomes.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the HGT detection pipeline results.

claims.claim: Different W/S-clade species subsequently retained different sets of genes after the surge of HGT events.
claims.source: Not excluding the possibility that independent events also occurred in the various species, this suggests that a surge of HGT events took place in the MRCA of the W/S clade and that different species subsequently retained different sets of genes, C. versatilis being the species that retained the most genes of bacterial origin (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the distribution of HGT-derived genes across species.

claims.claim: The horizontally transferred invertase appears to be the only enzyme with sucrose-hydrolyzing capacity encoded in the W/S-clade genomes investigated.
claims.source: In S. cerevisiae, the MAL and the IMA genes have also been shown to play a role in sucrose hydrolysis (Deng et al., 2014; Voordeckers et al., 2012), but these genes are absent in the genomes of W/S-clade species, meaning that the horizontally transferred invertase appears to be the only enzyme with sucrose-hydrolyzing capacity encoded in the W/S-clade genomes investigated.
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparative genomic analysis and citations.

claims.claim: Strong support for clustering of W/S-clade sequences to Acetobacteraceae SacC sequences was observed in the phylogenetic tree.
claims.source: In a phylogenetic tree reconstructed using the 200 top phmmer hits to W/S-clade species Candida magnoliae (protein ID 2301, see Figure 2—source data 2), strong support for clustering of W/S-clade sequences to Acetobacteraceae SacC sequences was observed (Figure 4A and Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: A topology comparison test strongly supported the HGT hypothesis for SUC2.
claims.source: A topology comparison test (Approximately Unbiased, AU) also strongly supported the HGT hypothesis (p-value=4e−07).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical topology test results.

claims.claim: Out of 43 proteins to which a GO molecular function was assigned, 16 impacted redox homeostasis and were associated with oxidoreductase activity and peroxidase activity.
claims.source: Notably, out of 43 proteins to which a GO molecular function was assigned, 16 impacted redox homeostasis and were associated with oxidoreductase activity (GO:0016491 and GO:0016616, 14 genes) and peroxidase activity (GO:004601, two genes), while a BLAST KOALA annotation (Kanehisa et al., 2016) indicated that the biological processes most frequently involved were amino acid metabolism, carbohydrate metabolism, and metabolism of cofactors and vitamins (Figure 2—source data 4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by GO annotation analysis.

claims.claim: The biological processes most frequently involved in the 52 ortholog groups were amino acid metabolism, carbohydrate metabolism, and metabolism of cofactors and vitamins.
claims.source: Notably, out of 43 proteins to which a GO molecular function was assigned, 16 impacted redox homeostasis and were associated with oxidoreductase activity (GO:0016491 and GO:0016616, 14 genes) and peroxidase activity (GO:004601, two genes), while a BLAST KOALA annotation (Kanehisa et al., 2016) indicated that the biological processes most frequently involved were amino acid metabolism, carbohydrate metabolism, and metabolism of cofactors and vitamins (Figure 2—source data 4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by BLAST KOALA annotation analysis.

claims.claim: In addition to ADH1, other alcohol dehydrogenase genes seem to have been horizontally acquired by W/S-clade species, including putative ADH6 and SFA1 orthologs.
claims.source: We noted that, in addition to ADH1, other alcohol dehydrogenase genes seem to have been horizontally acquired by W/S-clade species (Figure 2—source data 4), including putative ADH6 and SFA1 orthologs, which can also participate in alcoholic fermentation in S. cerevisiae (Drewke et al., 1990; Ida et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by HGT detection analysis and citations.

claims.claim: In all cases except for SFA1, the 'native' yeast orthologs appear to have been lost in W/S-clade genomes.
claims.source: In all cases, except for SFA1, the 'native' yeast orthologs appear to have been lost in W/S-clade genomes.
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparative genomic analysis.

claims.claim: All W/S-clade species clustered with strong support with the Acetobacteraceae Adh1 proteins.
claims.source: The resulting Adh1 tree (Figure 5A) included protein sequences from both bacteria and fungi. All W/S-clade species clustered with strong support with the Acetobacteraceae (Proteobacteria) Adh1 proteins (Figure 5A and Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Within the Adh1 W/S-clade cluster, the overall phylogenetic relationships were in line with the expected relationships between the species, suggesting that a single HGT event occurred in the MRCA of this clade.
claims.source: Within the Adh1 W/S-clade cluster, the overall phylogenetic relationships were in line with the expected relationships between the species (Figure 2A), suggesting that a single HGT event occurred in the MRCA of this clade.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic analysis.

claims.claim: Topology comparison tests strongly supported the Adh1 HGT event to the W/S clade.
claims.source: Topology comparison tests (AU) strongly supported the Adh1 HGT event to the W/S clade (p-value=8e−03), adding to the strong evidence of HGT provided by the robustly supported branch that clusters the W/S-clade xenologs with bacteria and the AI results.
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical topology test results.

claims.claim: The two Adh1 sequences from C. infanticola are not similar to those of the W/S clade.
claims.source: However, the two Adh1 sequences from C. infanticola are not similar to those of the W/S clade (Figure 5C), as might be expected if a single HGT event were responsible for the acquisition of the ADH1 gene in both lineages.
claims.evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: C. infanticola Adh1 sequences grouped with Adh1 sequences from the distantly related Lactobacillales and Enterobacteriales, implying that an independent HGT event may have occurred in the C. infanticola lineage.
claims.source: These sequences instead grouped, albeit with weak support, with Adh1 sequences from the distantly related Lactobacillales and Enterobacteriales (Figure 5C), implying that an independent HGT event may have occurred in the C. infanticola lineage.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: W/S-clade sequences clustered with strong support with Proteobacteria Adh6 sequences.
claims.source: In this phylogeny, W/S-clade sequences clustered with strong support (>95%) with Proteobacteria Adh6 sequences, within a large cluster that also encompasses known fungal Adh6 proteins.
claims.evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: While Adh1 W/S-clade sequences grouped with those of the Acetobacteraceae, the Adh6 sequences are more closely related to those of other bacterial families.
claims.source: Remarkably, while Adh1 W/S-clade sequences grouped with those of the Acetobacteraceae (Figure 5A and Figure 5B), the Adh6 sequences are more closely related to those of other bacterial families, as highlighted in Figure 6B.
claims.evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claims.claim: The absence of an ADH6 ortholog in C. infanticola was confirmed by a tBLASTx search.
claims.source: The absence of an ADH6 ortholog was further confirmed by a tBLASTx search against the C. infanticola genome using Adh6 sequences from both S. cerevisiae (KZV09178.1) and St. bombicola as queries.
claims.evidence: This is supported by tBLASTx search results.

claims.claim: Both ADH1 and ADH6 were lost in an ancestor of C. infanticola and the W/S clade.
claims.source: This result suggests that both ADH1 and ADH6 were lost in an ancestor of C. infanticola and the W/S clade.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of ADH6 in C. infanticola and the presence of bacterial versions in the W/S clade.

claims.claim: The ADH6 xenologs were apparently duplicated several times within each W/S-clade species.
claims.source: Interestingly, the ADH6 xenologs were apparently duplicated several times within each W/S-clade species (Figure 6A, Figure 6B and Figure 2—source data 4), and Starmerella bacillaris and C. magnoliae harbor the most paralogs (four in total).
claims.evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: Starmerella bacillaris and C. magnoliae harbor the most ADH6 paralogs (four in total).
claims.source: Interestingly, the ADH6 xenologs were apparently duplicated several times within each W/S-clade species (Figure 6A, Figure 6B and Figure 2—source data 4), and Starmerella bacillaris and C. magnoliae harbor the most paralogs (four in total).
claims.evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: All W/S-clade species tested were capable of using ethanol as carbon and energy source.
claims.source: All W/S-clade species tested were capable of using ethanol as carbon and energy source and have a Crabtree-negative behavior when growing on sugars, meaning that ethanol production in aerated batch cultures starts only when cell densities are very high,limiting oxygen availability (typically OD640 nm 30,~5–10 g/L ethanol in St. bombicola).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental observations.

claims.claim: W/S-clade species have a Crabtree-negative behavior when growing on sugars.
claims.source: All W/S-clade species tested were capable of using ethanol as carbon and energy source and have a Crabtree-negative behavior when growing on sugars, meaning that ethanol production in aerated batch cultures starts only when cell densities are very high,limiting oxygen availability (typically OD640 nm 30,~5–10 g/L ethanol in St. bombicola).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental observations.

claims.claim: In all non-W/S-clade species tested, the characteristic NADH-dependent Adh activity was readily observed, but no NADPH-dependent Adh activity was detected.
claims.source: In all non-W/S-clade species tested, the characteristic NADH-dependent Adh activity was readily observed, but no NADPH-dependent Adh activity was detected (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), in line with available information concerning yeast enzymes (Cho and Jeffries, 1998; Dashko et al., 2014; Ganzhorn et al., 1987; Leskovac et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and citations.

claims.claim: All W/S-clade species tested exhibited Adh activity when either NADH or NADPH was added to the reaction mixture.
claims.source: Conversely, all W/S-clade species tested (St. bombicola, C. magnoliae, and St. bacillaris) exhibited Adh activity when either NADH or NADPH was added to the reaction mixture (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: There was a lower affinity for the substrate (higher Km) for NADPH-dependent activity in St. bombicola.
claims.source: In fact, although both cofactors could be used for conversion of acetaldehyde into ethanol, there was a lower affinity for the substrate (higher Km) for NADPH-dependent activity in St. bombicola (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.

claims.claim: In Acetobacter pasteurianus, alcohol dehydrogenase activity was found to be NADH-dependent.
claims.source: Interestingly, in Acetobacter pasteurianus a bacterial species in the Acetobacteraceae, the same family as the likely donor of W/S-clade Adh1, alcohol dehydrogenase activity was found to be NADH-dependent, although it is unclear whether NADPH was also tested as a cofactor (Masud et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claims.claim: Deletion of ADH1 (adh1∆) did not significantly affect specific growth rates in glucose or fructose when compared to the wild type during aerated growth.
claims.source: During aerated growth, deletion of ADH1 (adh1∆) did not seem to significantly affect specific growth rates in glucose or fructose when compared to the wild type (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A.

claims.claim: There was a five-fold decrease in ethanol production in the adh1∆ mutant.
claims.source: However, we noted a five-fold decrease in ethanol production (Figure 7A) and the absence of growth on ethanol as sole carbon and energy source in the adh1∆ mutant (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: The adh1∆ mutant showed absence of growth on ethanol as sole carbon and energy source.
claims.source: However, we noted a five-fold decrease in ethanol production (Figure 7A) and the absence of growth on ethanol as sole carbon and energy source in the adh1∆ mutant (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: No Adh activity was detected in cell-free extracts of the adh1∆ mutant when either NADH or NADPH was used.
claims.source: Although some ethanol was produced, no Adh activity was detected in cell-free extracts of the adh1∆ mutant when either NADH or NADPH was used (Figure 5—figure supplement 2E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2E.

claims.claim: Adh1 is the main enzyme used in alcoholic fermentation in St. bombicola.
claims.source: These results suggest that Adh1 is the main enzyme used in alcoholic fermentation in St. bombicola and that it therefore likely accepts both NADH and NADPH as cofactors.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the phenotype of the adh1∆ mutant.

claims.claim: The significant decrease in ethanol yield in the adh1∆ mutant seems to be counterbalanced by a concomitant increase in glycerol production.
claims.source: In line with the cofactor preference measured in cell extracts, the significant decrease in ethanol yield seems to be counterbalanced by a concomitant increase in glycerol production (Figure 7A), similarly to what has been observed in the S. cerevisiae adh1∆ mutant (de Smidt et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A and citation.

claims.claim: Growth of the adh1∆ mutant cultivated on identical growth medium but under limited aeration was severely affected.
claims.source: Moreover, growth of the adh1∆ mutant cultivated on identical growth medium but under limited aeration was severely affected (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3B.

claims.claim: Adh1 plays an important role in redox homeostasis, namely in NAD+ regeneration in the absence of oxygen.
claims.source: Taken together, these observations strongly suggest that Adh1 plays an important role in redox homeostasis, namely in NAD+ regeneration in the absence of oxygen because, similarly to S. cerevisiae, glycerol formation in St. bombicola is probably a NAD+ regenerating reaction.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the phenotypes of the adh1∆ mutant and comparison to S. cerevisiae.

claims.claim: NADP+ dependent glycerol dehydrogenase activity was not detected in cell-free extracts of St. bombicola.
claims.source: Consistent with this hypothesis, we did not detect NADP+ dependent glycerol dehydrogenase activity in cell-free extracts (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D), and in at least one W/S-clade species, this reaction was shown to be NADH-dependent (Van Bogaert et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D and citation.

claims.claim: Mannitol production was significantly decreased in the adh1∆ mutant.
claims.source: In contrast, mannitol production, which is a NADP+ regenerating reaction (Lee et al., 2003b), was significantly decreased in the adh1∆ mutant (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A and citation.

claims.claim: The deletion of each of the two ADH6 paralogous genes (adh6a∆ and adh6b∆ mutants) did not significantly affect ethanol production.
claims.source: The deletion of each of the two ADH6 paralogous genes (adh6a∆ and adh6b∆ mutants) did not significantly affect ethanol production (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: When Adh1 is functional, Adh6a and Adh6b are not essential for ethanol metabolism and are probably mainly involved in other metabolic reactions.
claims.source: This means that, although some of the enzymes encoded by these genes might be involved in the production of ethanol in the absence of Adh1, when Adh1 is functional, they are not essential for ethanol metabolism and are probably mainly involved in other metabolic reactions.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the phenotypes of the adh6a∆ and adh6b∆ mutants.

claims.claim: There was a significant decrease in sugar consumption rates in the adh1∆ mutant.
claims.source: There was a significant decrease in sugar consumption rates in the adh1∆ mutant (Figure 7B), but fructophily was still observed in all mutants and became even more pronounced as the lack of Adh1 affected glucose consumption more than it did fructose consumption.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: Fructophily was still observed in all mutants (adh1∆, adh6a∆, and adh6b∆) and became even more pronounced as the lack of Adh1 affected glucose consumption more than it did fructose consumption.
claims.source: There was a significant decrease in sugar consumption rates in the adh1∆ mutant (Figure 7B), but fructophily was still observed in all mutants and became even more pronounced as the lack of Adh1 affected glucose consumption more than it did fructose consumption.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: The aro10Δ mutant failed to produce ethanol.
claims.source: This mutant failed to produce ethanol, as might be expected in the complete absence of pyruvate decarboxylase activity (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: The aro10Δ mutant exhibited increased glycerol production.
claims.source: Similarly to the adh1Δ mutant, it exhibited increased glycerol production, but unlike the former, it grew considerably slower than the wild type strain in aerated conditions (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A and 7C.

claims.claim: The aro10Δ mutant grew considerably slower than the wild type strain in aerated conditions.
claims.source: Similarly to the adh1Δ mutant, it exhibited increased glycerol production, but unlike the former, it grew considerably slower than the wild type strain in aerated conditions (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: The decrease in growth rate in the aro10Δ mutant was probably mainly due to the fact that the absence of pyruvate decarboxylase activity affects other metabolic routes in addition to alcoholic fermentation, such as the production of acetate and acetoin.
claims.source: This decrease was probably mainly due to the fact that the absence of pyruvate decarboxylase activity affects other metabolic routes in addition to alcoholic fermentation, such as the production of acetate and acetoin (Flikweert et al., 1996).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the phenotype and citation to prior literature.

claims.claim: Aro10 is the only decarboxylase involved in alcoholic fermentation in St. bombicola.
claims.source: The phenotype observed in this mutant confirmed that Aro10 is the only decarboxylase involved in alcoholic fermentation in St. bombicola and that, therefore, the modification of enzymatic specificities was also involved in remodeling alcoholic fermentation in W/S-clade yeasts.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the phenotype of the aro10Δ mutant.

claims.claim: The modification of enzymatic specificities was involved in remodeling alcoholic fermentation in W/S-clade yeasts.
claims.source: The phenotype observed in this mutant confirmed that Aro10 is the only decarboxylase involved in alcoholic fermentation in St. bombicola and that, therefore, the modification of enzymatic specificities was also involved in remodeling alcoholic fermentation in W/S-clade yeasts.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the phenotype of the aro10Δ mutant and the phylogenetic relationship of Aro10 to S. cerevisiae Aro10.

claims.claim: In the aro10∆ mutant, glucose consumption seems to be even more seriously affected than in the adh1Δ mutant.
claims.source: Importantly, in the aro10∆ mutant, glucose consumption seems to be even more seriously affected than in the adh1Δ mutant (Figure 7B) and, in fact, glucose was left all but untouched even after 120 hr of growth (Figure 7C), while fructose was almost totally consumed.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B and 7C.

claims.claim: In the aro10∆ mutant, glucose was left all but untouched even after 120 hr of growth, while fructose was almost totally consumed.
claims.source: Importantly, in the aro10∆ mutant, glucose consumption seems to be even more seriously affected than in the adh1Δ mutant (Figure 7B) and, in fact, glucose was left all but untouched even after 120 hr of growth (Figure 7C), while fructose was almost totally consumed.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: All publicly available genomes across the entire subphylum Saccharomycotina possess at least one ADH1 ortholog.
claims.source: In fact, all publicly available genomes across the entire subphylum Saccharomycotina possess at least one ADH1 ortholog.
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of publicly available genomes.

claims.claim: Candida galacta lacks both PDC1 and ADH1.
claims.source: Remarkably, sequencing of the genome of Candida galacta (Figure 8) in the context of a distinct project (the Y1000+ Project sequencing the genomes of all known species of Saccharomycotina; http://y1000plus.org)(Hittinger et al., 2015) showed that it lacks both PDC1 and ADH1 (Figure 8, Figure 2—source data 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by genome sequencing data shown in Figure 8 and Figure 2—source data 3.

claims.claim: The phylogenetic position of C. galacta strongly supports the hypothesis that loss of native ADH1 preceded the acquisition of the bacterial versions of the gene by the C. infanticola lineage and by the MRCA of the W/S clade.
claims.source: The phylogenetic position of this species strongly supports the hypothesis that loss of native ADH1 preceded the (likely independent) acquisition of the bacterial versions of the gene by the C. infanticola lineage and by the MRCA of the W/S clade.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the phylogenetic position of C. galacta and its lack of ADH1 and PDC1.

claims.claim: The presence of xenologs involved in alcoholic fermentation in extant W/S-clade yeasts can be best explained by the need to restore alcoholic fermentation in a lineage that had previously lost it.
claims.source: In conclusion, given the evidence presented here, the presence of xenologs involved in alcoholic fermentation in extant W/S-clade yeasts can be best explained by the need to restore alcoholic fermentation in a lineage that had previously lost it.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The involvement of bacterial genes in restoring alcoholic fermentation seems to have been circumstantial and possibly a consequence of the availability of the donor in the same environment.
claims.source: In this case, the involvement of bacterial genes seems to have been circumstantial and possibly a consequence of the availability of the donor in the same environment.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the ecological context.

claims.claim: W/S-clade Adh1 proteins are most closely related to those of a bacterial lineage that is also frequently associated with the floral niche (Acetobacteraceae).
claims.source: The ecological opportunity for the horizontal exchange of genetic material underlying the acquisition of bacterial ADH1 seems to have existed for a long time, since W/S-clade Adh1 proteins are most closely related to those of a bacterial lineage that is also frequently associated with the floral niche (Acetobacteraceae) (Iino et al., 2012; Suzuki et al., 2010; Tucker and Fukami, 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis and citations about the ecology of Acetobacteraceae.

claims.claim: Evolution of 'native' SUC2 seems to be punctuated by multiple loss events resulting in a patchy extant distribution.
claims.source: Unlike the 'native' version of ADH1, which is ubiquitous in the Saccharomycotina except in the W/S clade, evolution of 'native' SUC2 seems to be punctuated by multiple loss events resulting in a patchy extant distribution (Carlson et al., 1985), which is probably linked to its role as a 'social' gene (Sanchez and Gore, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: The basis for fructophily arose in yeasts in a lineage devoid of alcoholic fermentation, but probably well equipped to use fructose as electron acceptor with concomitant production of mannitol.
claims.source: Taken together, our results suggest the enticing hypothesis that the basis for fructophily arose in yeasts in a lineage devoid of alcoholic fermentation, but probably well equipped to use fructose as electron acceptor with concomitant production of mannitol (Baek et al., 2010; Lee et al., 2003a), through the horizontal acquisition of the Ffz1 transporter that enabled the efficient utilization of fructose as carbon and energy source.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the findings of the study and citations.

claims.claim: A putative ancestor lineage would resemble the aro10∆ mutant in that it would be unable to use glucose in high-sugar conditions.
claims.source: Such a lineage would resemble the aro10∆ mutant in that it would be unable to use glucose in high-sugar conditions.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the phenotype of the aro10∆ mutant.

claims.claim: The putative ancestor might subsequently have acquired fermentative capacity to enable efficient glucose consumption and SUC2 to permit the utilization of sucrose.
claims.source: This putative ancestor might subsequently have acquired fermentative capacity to enable efficient glucose consumption and SUC2 to permit the utilization of sucrose, thereby completing the set of tools required to use the sugars abundant in the floral niche.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about the evolutionary trajectory.

claims.claim: Fructophilic yeasts seem to have been able to overcome the inability to use glucose efficiently, as observed in extant fructophilic bacteria.
claims.source: In conclusion, our previous (Gonçalves et al., 2016) and present results uncovered, to our knowledge for the first time, an instance of major remodeling of central carbon metabolism in fungi involving the horizontal acquisition of a multitude of genes mostly from bacteria. Thereby, fructophilic yeasts seem to have been able to overcome the inability to use glucose efficiently, as observed in extant fructophilic bacteria.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the findings of the study.

claims.claim: The suc2∆ mutants were unable to grow on sucrose as sole carbon and energy source.
claims.source: Growth assays in medium supplemented with sucrose as sole carbon and energy source, showed that suc2∆ mutants were unable to grow (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), while the wild-type strain attained high-cell densities.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: The suc2∆ mutant failed to consume measurable amounts of sucrose, even after 72 hr.
claims.source: Furthermore, the suc2∆ mutant failed to consume measurable amounts of sucrose, even after 72 hr (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: During growth of the wild-type strain on sucrose, the decrease in sucrose concentrations was accompanied by the appearance of fructose and glucose in the growth medium, strongly suggesting that the horizontally transferred SUC2 gene encodes an extracellular invertase.
claims.source: During growth of the wild-type strain on sucrose, the decrease in sucrose concentrations was accompanied by the appearance of fructose and glucose in the growth medium, strongly suggesting that the horizontally transferred SUC2 gene encodes an extracellular invertase (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: The apparent absence of genes encoding sucrose transporters in the W/S-clade genomes analyzed indicates that sucrose must be first hydrolyzed outside the cell to be used as a carbon and energy source.
claims.source: This conclusion is consistent with the apparent absence of genes encoding sucrose transporters in the W/S-clade genomes analyzed, which indicates that sucrose must be first hydrolyzed outside the cell to be used as a carbon and energy source.

claims.claim: St. bombicola is a species used for the production of sophorolipids, which are amphipathic molecules that are employed as biosurfactants.
claims.source: The most prominent example is St. bombicola, a species used for the production of sophorolipids, which are amphipathic molecules that are employed as biosurfactants (Samad et al., 2015; Takahashi et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.source: Starmerella bacillaris is often found in wine fermentations and is known for diverting an important fraction of its carbon flux towards the production of glycerol instead of ethanol (Englezos et al., 2015).

claims.source: Candida magnoliae has been reported to be capable of producing large amounts of erythritol (Ryu et al., 2000).

claims.claim: Site-directed mutagenesis of a few selected sites was capable of considerably increasing the affinity of S. cerevisiae Aro10 for pyruvate.
claims.source: However, it has been shown that site-directed mutagenesis of a few selected sites was capable of considerably increasing the affinity of S. cerevisiae Aro10 for pyruvate (Kneen et al., 2011), which supports the notion that this shift in substrate specificity may have occurred naturally in the course of evolution of W/S-clade yeasts.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

results.result: The Ffz1 transporter is essential for fructophily in Starmerella bombicola. Deletion of FFZ1 completely abolished fructophilic behavior and slightly increased glucose consumption rate in the ffz1Δ mutant.
results.evaluation: Claims C25 and C26 are directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1, demonstrating that deletion of FFZ1 eliminates preferential fructose consumption and modestly increases glucose consumption. This provides clear genetic evidence for the role of Ffz1 in fructophily.

results.result: W/S-clade species and C. infanticola possess Adh1 homologs of bacterial origin, distinct from the native fungal ADH1 found in non-fructophilic yeasts. BLAST analyses show that W/S-clade Adh1 sequences are much less similar to S. cerevisiae ADH1 and cluster with bacterial proteins.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C32 are supported by tBLASTx and BLASTp results shown in Figure 2B. The sequence similarity metrics (E-value, identity, bitscore) and the observation that top 1000 BLAST hits are bacterial proteins provide strong computational evidence for bacterial origin of ADH1 in the W/S clade.

results.result: PDC1 was lost in the W/S clade and replaced by ARO10-like decarboxylases. Pdc sequences from W/S-clade species are more dissimilar to S. cerevisiae Pdc1 and cluster with Aro10 proteins, while C. versatilis possesses bacterial-origin Pdc1 genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C35, C37-C38 are supported by tBLASTx results (Figure 2B) and phylogenetic analysis (Figure 3). The phylogenetic clustering of W/S-clade sequences with fungal Aro10 proteins and C. versatilis sequences with bacterial pyruvate decarboxylases provides strong evidence for the evolutionary trajectory described.

results.result: A surge of horizontal gene transfer (HGT) events from bacteria occurred in the most recent common ancestor (MRCA) of the W/S clade. W/S-clade species possess considerably more HGT-derived genes than closely related species, with 52 ortholog groups identified across multiple W/S-clade genomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C45 are supported by Alien Index analysis (Figure 2A, Figure 2—source data 2) showing elevated numbers of bacterial-origin genes in W/S-clade species. The identification of 52 ortholog groups present in multiple W/S species supports the inference of a surge of HGT in the MRCA, though alternative explanations of independent HGT events cannot be fully excluded.

results.result: The W/S clade acquired a bacterial invertase (SUC2) essential for sucrose utilization. Phylogenetic analysis shows strong clustering with Acetobacteraceae sequences, and deletion mutants cannot grow on or consume sucrose.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C48 and C103-C106 are supported by phylogenetic analysis (Figure 4) showing strong support for bacterial origin (AU test p-value=4e-07) and experimental data (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) demonstrating that suc2Δ mutants cannot grow on or consume sucrose. The appearance of fructose and glucose during wild-type growth on sucrose supports the extracellular invertase function.

results.result: ADH1 was horizontally transferred from Acetobacteraceae to the MRCA of the W/S clade in a single event. C. infanticola acquired ADH1 independently from different bacterial lineages (Lactobacillales/Enterobacteriales).
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C57 are supported by phylogenetic analysis (Figure 5) showing strong clustering of W/S-clade sequences with Acetobacteraceae (bootstrap >95%) and topology tests (AU p-value=8e-03). The phylogenetic relationships within the W/S clade match expected species relationships, supporting a single HGT event. C. infanticola sequences cluster separately, suggesting independent acquisition, though support is weak.

results.result: ADH6 was horizontally transferred from Proteobacteria to the W/S clade and subsequently duplicated multiple times within species. ADH6 is absent in C. infanticola, suggesting both ADH1 and ADH6 were lost in a common ancestor.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C63 are supported by phylogenetic analysis (Figure 6) showing strong clustering (>95% bootstrap) with Proteobacteria Adh6 sequences from different bacterial families than ADH1. The absence of ADH6 in C. infanticola confirmed by tBLASTx supports the inference of ancestral loss. Multiple paralogs in W/S species are evident in the phylogeny.

results.result: W/S-clade alcohol dehydrogenases exhibit dual cofactor specificity, accepting both NADH and NADPH, unlike native yeast enzymes that are NADH-specific. NADPH-dependent activity shows lower substrate affinity in St. bombicola.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C68 are supported by enzymatic assays (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A-C) showing NADH-only activity in non-W/S species and dual cofactor activity in W/S-clade species. Kinetic measurements demonstrate higher Km for NADPH-dependent activity, indicating lower affinity. This represents a functional characterization of the bacterial-origin enzymes.

results.result: Adh1 is the main enzyme responsible for alcoholic fermentation in St. bombicola. The adh1Δ mutant shows a five-fold decrease in ethanol production, cannot grow on ethanol, and has no detectable Adh activity with either NADH or NADPH.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C74 are supported by experimental data showing growth rates (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A), ethanol production (Figure 7A), ethanol utilization (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), and enzyme activity assays (Figure 5—figure supplement 2E). The complete loss of detectable Adh activity despite some residual ethanol production strongly supports Adh1 as the main fermentative enzyme.

results.result: Adh1 plays a critical role in redox homeostasis and NAD+ regeneration. In the adh1Δ mutant, decreased ethanol production is compensated by increased glycerol production (NAD+ regenerating) and decreased mannitol production (NADP+ regenerating), with severe growth defects under limited aeration.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C79 are supported by metabolite production data (Figure 7A), growth under limited aeration (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B), and glycerol dehydrogenase assays (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D). The pattern of metabolic compensation is consistent with Adh1 primarily functioning in NAD+ regeneration, similar to S. cerevisiae.

results.result: ADH6 paralogs (Adh6a and Adh6b) are not essential for ethanol metabolism when Adh1 is functional. Deletion of ADH6 genes does not significantly affect ethanol production, and fructophily persists in all mutants with glucose consumption more affected than fructose consumption.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C83 are supported by experimental data showing ethanol production (Figure 7A) and sugar consumption rates (Figure 7B) in adh6aΔ and adh6bΔ mutants. The lack of significant phenotype for ADH6 deletions contrasts with the strong adh1Δ phenotype, supporting the inference that Adh6 enzymes play minor roles in fermentation when Adh1 is present.

results.result: Aro10 is the only decarboxylase involved in alcoholic fermentation in St. bombicola. The aro10Δ mutant completely fails to produce ethanol, exhibits increased glycerol production, and grows slower than wild-type, confirming that enzymatic specificity modification was involved in remodeling fermentation.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C89 are supported by experimental data showing complete absence of ethanol production (Figure 7A), increased glycerol production, and reduced growth rate (Figure 7C) in the aro10Δ mutant. The complete loss of ethanol production confirms Aro10 as the sole pyruvate decarboxylase for fermentation, supporting the modification of enzymatic specificity hypothesis.

results.result: In the aro10Δ mutant, glucose consumption is severely impaired while fructose consumption continues. After 120 hours, glucose remains largely unconsumed while fructose is almost completely consumed.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C91 are supported by experimental data (Figure 7B and 7C) showing differential effects on glucose versus fructose consumption in the aro10Δ mutant. This striking phenotype suggests a specific link between pyruvate decarboxylase activity and glucose metabolism in high-sugar conditions.

results.result: Candida galacta lacks both PDC1 and ADH1 genes. Its phylogenetic position strongly supports the hypothesis that loss of native ADH1 and PDC1 preceded acquisition of bacterial versions in the W/S clade and C. infanticola lineages.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C94 are supported by genome sequencing data (Figure 8, Figure 2—source data 3) showing absence of both genes and phylogenetic placement of C. galacta between C. infanticola and the W/S clade. This provides critical evidence for the 'loss followed by reacquisition' hypothesis, as C. galacta represents an extant lineage lacking these genes.

results.result: Alcoholic fermentation was lost in an ancestor of the W/S clade and subsequently reinstated through horizontal acquisition of bacterial genes (ADH1, ADH6, and in some species PDC1) and modification of a pre-existing yeast gene (ARO10).
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C4 and C95 represent the central conclusion of the manuscript, supported by multiple lines of evidence: (1) identification of C. galacta lacking both ADH1 and PDC1 (C93-C94), (2) phylogenetic evidence for bacterial origin of ADH1 and ADH6 (C53-C63), (3) functional characterization showing these genes perform fermentation functions (C70-C89), and (4) phylogenetic evidence that W/S-clade Pdc is Aro10-like (C37). The convergence of genomic, phylogenetic, and functional evidence strongly supports this major remodeling of central carbon metabolism.

results.result: The acquisition of fructophily in the W/S clade is concurrent with a wider remodeling of central carbon metabolism, likely related to adaptation to high-sugar environments. This demonstrates that central carbon metabolism can be remodeled by a surge of HGT events.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C6, and C7 represent overarching conclusions supported by the collective evidence: acquisition of Ffz1 for fructose transport (C25), loss and reacquisition of fermentation genes (C3-C4), acquisition of SUC2 for sucrose utilization (C47-C48), and the surge of HGT events (C41-C45). The ecological context (floral niche, C15) and functional characterization of acquired genes support the adaptation hypothesis, though the mechanistic link between fructophily and fermentation remodeling remains somewhat speculative.

results.result: Among 52 ortholog groups of bacterial origin in the W/S clade, 16 out of 43 with assigned GO functions impact redox homeostasis (oxidoreductase and peroxidase activity). The most frequent biological processes are amino acid metabolism, carbohydrate metabolism, and metabolism of cofactors and vitamins.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C50 are supported by GO annotation and BLAST KOALA analysis (Figure 2—source data 4). The enrichment for redox-related functions is consistent with the hypothesis linking metabolic remodeling to redox homeostasis, though the functional significance of many of these genes remains to be experimentally validated.

results.result: All glycolytic genes are present in W/S-clade species with expected similarity to S. cerevisiae, and high-quality genome assemblies make it unlikely that alcoholic fermentation genes were missed due to assembly issues.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C40 are supported by comparative genomic analysis (Figure 2—source data 3) and quality assessment of genome assemblies. This addresses a potential technical concern about the absence of ADH1 and PDC1, strengthening the conclusion that these genes were genuinely lost rather than missed due to sequencing/assembly artifacts.

results.result: The horizontally transferred invertase is the only sucrose-hydrolyzing enzyme in W/S-clade genomes (MAL and IMA genes are absent), and native yeast orthologs of ADH1, ADH6, and PDC1 were lost (except SFA1 for ADH).
results.evaluation: Claims C46 and C52 are supported by comparative genomic analysis showing absence of alternative sucrose metabolism genes and native fermentation genes. This supports the conclusion that the bacterial-origin genes are not redundant additions but replacements for lost native genes.

results.result: All W/S-clade species tested can use ethanol as a carbon source and exhibit Crabtree-negative behavior, producing ethanol only at high cell densities when oxygen becomes limiting.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C65 are supported by experimental observations of growth on ethanol and ethanol production patterns. This metabolic characterization provides context for understanding the role of the acquired fermentation genes and distinguishes W/S-clade metabolism from Crabtree-positive yeasts like S. cerevisiae.

results.result: All publicly available genomes across the entire subphylum Saccharomycotina possess at least one ADH1 ortholog, with the exception of C. galacta and W/S-clade species (which have bacterial versions).
results.evaluation: Claim C92 is supported by analysis of publicly available genomes. This establishes the ubiquity of ADH1 in yeasts and highlights the exceptional nature of its loss in the lineage leading to the W/S clade, strengthening the significance of the findings.

results.result: In addition to ADH1, other alcohol dehydrogenase genes (ADH6 and SFA1) were horizontally acquired by W/S-clade species, and these can participate in alcoholic fermentation in S. cerevisiae.
results.evaluation: Claim C51 is supported by HGT detection analysis (Figure 2—source data 4) and citations to prior literature about S. cerevisiae enzyme functions. However, the functional role of SFA1 in W/S-clade species was not experimentally tested in this study.

results.result: In Acetobacter pasteurianus (Acetobacteraceae, the likely donor family of W/S-clade Adh1), alcohol dehydrogenase activity is NADH-dependent, though it is unclear if NADPH was tested.
results.evaluation: Claim C69 is supported by citation to prior literature (Masud et al., 2011). This provides context for the cofactor specificity of W/S-clade Adh1 enzymes, though the uncertainty about whether NADPH was tested in the bacterial enzyme limits the comparison.

results.result: W/S-clade Adh1 proteins are most closely related to Acetobacteraceae, a bacterial lineage frequently associated with the floral niche, suggesting ecological opportunity for horizontal gene transfer.
results.evaluation: Claim C97 is supported by phylogenetic analysis (Figure 5) and citations about Acetobacteraceae ecology. This provides a plausible ecological context for the HGT event, though direct evidence of co-occurrence in the same floral environments is not provided.

results.result: The involvement of bacterial genes in restoring alcoholic fermentation was circumstantial and possibly a consequence of donor availability in the same environment.
results.evaluation: Claim C96 is speculative (as noted in evidence_type). While the ecological co-occurrence of W/S-clade yeasts and Acetobacteraceae in floral niches is documented (C97), there is no direct evidence that the HGT occurred due to environmental proximity rather than functional selection for specific enzymatic properties. The dual cofactor specificity of the acquired enzymes could represent a functional advantage.

results.result: The authors hypothesize that fructophily arose in a lineage lacking alcoholic fermentation but capable of using fructose as an electron acceptor (producing mannitol), resembling the aro10Δ mutant. This ancestor subsequently acquired fermentative capacity and SUC2.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C101 represent a speculative evolutionary scenario based on the phenotype of the aro10Δ mutant (C90-C91) and known mannitol production in W/S species. While the scenario is plausible and consistent with the data, it remains a hypothesis about the temporal order of events that cannot be definitively tested with the current evidence. The link between loss of fermentation and acquisition of fructophily is inferred but not directly demonstrated.

results.result: Fructophily is a rare trait involving preference for fructose, and the Ffz1 transporter is intimately associated with fructophily in yeasts. Prior work established correlation between Ffz1 presence and fructophily, genetic requirement in Z. rouxii, and that FFZ1 alone is insufficient for fructophily.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C13-C15, and C21-C24 summarize prior work by the authors and others, supported by citations. These establish the context and motivation for the current study. The current work (C25) confirms the requirement for FFZ1 in St. bombicola, extending prior findings in Z. rouxii.

results.result: Prior literature establishes that horizontal gene transfer (HGT) has played important roles in fungal domestication, metabolism evolution, and adaptation to new environments, with frequent transfer of genes encoding nutrient transporters and metabolic gene clusters.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C12 summarize established knowledge from prior literature, supported by appropriate citations. These provide the broader context for understanding the significance of HGT in the W/S clade.

results.result: Fructophilic lactic acid bacteria in the floral niche grow poorly on glucose due to lack of respiratory chain enzymes and alcohol dehydrogenase, and use fructose as both carbon source and electron acceptor. Fructophily in bacteria is linked to redox homeostasis, unlike in yeasts which grow well on glucose alone.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C20 summarize prior work on bacterial fructophily, supported by citations. This provides important comparative context for understanding yeast fructophily and motivates investigation of redox homeostasis in the W/S clade.

results.result: Prior work established that some W/S-clade yeasts produce sugar alcohols or lipids instead of ethanol, that S. cerevisiae ADH1 encodes the main enzyme for acetaldehyde-to-ethanol conversion, and that S. cerevisiae Aro10 acts on substrates other than pyruvate and is not involved in fermentation.
results.evaluation: Claims C27, C28, and C36 summarize established knowledge from prior literature, supported by citations. These provide essential background for interpreting the findings about ADH1 and ARO10 in the W/S clade.

results.result: Prior work shows that native SUC2 has a patchy distribution due to multiple losses, W/S-clade species have various biotechnological applications, S. cerevisiae Aro10 can be engineered for pyruvate affinity, and metabolic pathway loss/reacquisition via HGT occurred in red algae.
results.evaluation: Claims C98, C107-C111 summarize prior literature providing context for the findings. C110 is particularly relevant as it supports the plausibility of natural Aro10 specificity changes. C111 provides a precedent for the type of metabolic remodeling observed in the W/S clade.

results.result: Fructophilic yeasts overcame the inability to use glucose efficiently that is observed in extant fructophilic bacteria, representing a major remodeling of central carbon metabolism through horizontal acquisition of bacterial genes.
results.evaluation: Claim C102 represents a concluding statement supported by the collective findings. W/S-clade yeasts maintain fructophily (C25) while retaining the ability to grow on glucose (C20), unlike fructophilic bacteria (C17). The remodeling involved acquisition of bacterial fermentation genes (C3-C4) and other metabolic genes (C41-C45), distinguishing yeast fructophily from bacterial fructophily.
